newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia analysts see rate cut-IBSA survey.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia analysts see rate cut-IBSA survey.

text.p: Australian economists are generally forecasting another cut in official interest rates by the end of the year but are less sure on the outlook for the Australian dollar, the International Banks and Securities Association of Australia (IBSA) said.
In its latest quarterly survey of member bank economists released Thursday, IBSA found only two out of 11 were not looking for another easing in monetary policy.
"Continued patchy economic growth and the favourable outlook for inflation should allow the Reserve Bank to cut rates," said Ric Simes, chief economist at Rothschild Australia.
Official rates are presently at 7.00 percent, having been cut by 0.50 point on July 31.
The economists expected headline inflation to fall below the underlying rate over the next few quarters to around 2.00 percent on average.

"A very sharp drop in headline inflation occurs from this quarter's figures as previous taxation rises drop out, the benefits of the A$ appreciation accrue, and recent mortgage rate reductions are reflected in the figures," said Ivan Colhoun, an associate director at Bain. "We expect headline inflation around 1.5 percent in each of the December and March quarters."
The headline consumer price index stood at 3.1 percent in the June quarter.
Economists were divided on where the Australian dollar was heading with forecasts ranging from as low as 72 U.S. cents to as high as 83 cents by the end of the March quarter.
"The A$ has got ahead of the commodity price story," said Chris Caton, chief economist sat Bankers Trust Australia who sees the dollar at 77 cents in the next two quarters.
"The currency is now 18 percent above its mid-1995 trough but the RBA index of commodity prices has risen by less than 10 percent," he said.
Yasushi Usuda, an economist at Tokai Finance Australia, saw the dollar declining to 75 cents by the March quarter partly due to fear of another interest rate cut here.
The Australian dollar was around US$0.7910 at midday on Thursday.

However, Citbank Australia's senior economist Stephen Koukoulas was more optimistic, predicting a rise to 83 cents by the March quarter on relative gains in the current account deficit and favourable fundamentals.

The yield on 10-year Commonwealth bonds was generally expected to remain around its current 7.84 percent. Caton at Bankers Trust said the yield differential against 10-year U.S. Treasuries had already priced in a lot of good news.
"The differential was 240 basis points in April; it is now less than half of that," he said.
The yield gap at midday Thursday was 109 basis points.
